title_en: General Fatwas on Purification and Prayer
body_ar:
حكم الوضوء قبل دخول الوقت هل يجزئ الوضوء للصلاة قبل دخول الوقت؟

أنه أفضل، فبقاء الإنسان على طهارة دائما إن استطاع من فضائل الأعمال، وهو سبب سبق بلال إلى الجنة، فقد كان كلما أحدث توضأ وكلما توضأ صلى ركعتين.

--------------------------------------

حكم من لا يستطيع تحريك يمينه امرأة مصابة بمرض عصبي لا تستطيع الوقوف بنفسها ولا تتصرف بيمينها هل يسقط عنها الوضوء إذا أرادت الصلاة؟

ما دامت تجد من يساعدها على الوضوء ويقوم بغسل أعضاء الوضوء فلا يسقط عنها الوضوء، بل ربما يكون من علاجها وسببا لشفائها إن شاء الله، وإذا لم تجد من يساعدها في ذلك فلا يكلف الله نفسا إلا وسعها.
body_en:
The ruling on performing ablution before the time of the prayer has come in. Does ablution for the prayer suffice before the time has come in?

It is better. A person's remaining always in a state of ritual purity, if he is able to, is among the meritorious deeds (faḍāʾil al-aʿmāl); and it was the cause of Bilal's going ahead into the Garden, for whenever he broke his ablution he performed ablution, and whenever he performed ablution he prayed two units of prayer.

--------------------------------------

The ruling on one who cannot move her right hand. A woman afflicted with a nerve disease who cannot stand by herself and cannot use her right hand — is ablution waived for her if she wishes to pray?

So long as she finds someone to help her with the ablution and to wash the limbs of ablution for her, ablution is not waived for her; rather it may be part of her treatment and a cause of her cure, God willing. And if she does not find anyone to help her in that, then God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.

flags.arabic: وإذا لم تجد من يساعدها في ذلك فلا يكلف الله نفسا إلا وسعها
flags.context: the closing sentence of the second fatwa
options: render faithfully and mark that the alternative is never named
read it as waiving the prayer
flags.note: CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY — STYLE GUIDE §10. The Sheikh answers the case where help is available and then, for the case where it is not, quotes a verse and stops. He does not say what the woman actually does — whether she performs dry ablution (tayammum), or prays as she is, or anything else. Since that is the practical question, a reader in her position is left without an answer, and an English reader may easily take the verse for a waiver of the prayer itself. Nothing has been supplied. The site must not present this as a complete answer.

flags.context: the answer to whether ablution before the prayer time suffices
options: It is valid, and indeed better
flags.note: The question asks whether ablution before the prayer time SUFFICES — a question of validity. The Sheikh answers 'it is better', which is a statement about merit, and he does not say in so many words that it is valid, though the answer implies it. Neither 'valid' nor a five-rulings term has been supplied. Note that he does use a graded Maliki term two clauses later, faḍāʾil al-aʿmāl, which the glossary fixes as 'meritorious act' for faḍīlah and which is a grade below sunnah.

flags.arabic: فلا يكلف الله نفسا إلا وسعها
flags.context: the verse quoted at the close of the second fatwa
options: render without Qur'anic braces, as the source does, and note the reference
set in curly braces per house style and supply the reference
render as the Sheikh's own words
flags.note: The wording is Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:286, but the source gives it unmarked, running on from the Sheikh's own sentence with no quotation marks or braces, so that a reader cannot tell where his words end and the verse begins. Preserved as the source has it in body_ar. A reviewer should decide whether the site marks it as scripture; the reference is recorded here either way.

Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.

EXCERPT ONLY. The page publishes the opening and breaks off; the full text sits behind the .docx download recorded in source_download_link. The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends. The site must render this with an excerpt banner, never as a whole article.
Each of the two fatwas opens with a sub-heading in the source which then runs directly into the question; both have been kept as the source has them.
The account of Bilal is given without narrator, collection or grading; nothing has been supplied.
'Breaks his ablution' renders aḥdatha, from ḥadath, the state of ritual impurity, per the glossary.
